sections.title: Deepening the reflexive/-ik verb family
sections.content: You know *-ik* verbs such as *ismerkedik* (A2 Unit 5) and *megoldódik* (A2 Unit 31), and the reflexive *érzem magam* ("I feel [myself]"). Hungarian has a second, much larger family: verbs built with endings like *-kodik/-kedik/-ködik*, or older-looking forms like *veszekedik* and *összevész*, that describe an action the subject does that is self-contained — it doesn't reach out to a direct object the way *eszik kenyeret* does. *veszekedik* ("to argue, quarrel") and *összevész valakivel* ("to fall out with someone") both work this way: the other person is never a direct object, always marked with *-val/-vel*.

sections.title: Arguing and falling out
rows: I fell out with my friend

items.english: They argue a lot these days.
Yesterday I fell out with my best friend.
Who did you fall out with?

sections.content: Don't reach for an accusative object with these verbs — you never *veszekedik valakit* or *összevész valakit*. Both take *-val/-vel*: *veszekedem veled*, *összevesztem vele*. Notice that *összevész* keeps *össze-* in front in a plain statement (*Összevesztem vele*) and splits after a question word or *nem* (*Kivel vesztél össze?*), the same way any *igekötő* verb does.
